title: Plasma
objective: After this level you can explain plasma, the state of matter in lightning and the Sun.
summary: Heat a gas enough, or hit it with lightning, and electrons break free, making plasma: a gas of charged particles. Stars are mostly plasma, so nearly all visible matter is plasma.

cards.headline: Lightning heats air to about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
cards.body: The air in a lightning channel can reach about 50,000 °F. That air stops being an ordinary gas and becomes a fourth state of matter, one you rarely meet on Earth but the universe is full of.

cards.fact: Plasma is a gas with its electrons torn loose.
cards.context: Heat a gas enough and its atoms crash together so hard that electrons, tiny charged particles from inside atoms, get knocked free. High-voltage electricity like lightning can do the same. What's left is a gas full of electrically charged particles, so plasma conducts electricity. Chemists count it as the fourth state of matter, after solid, liquid and gas.

cards.headline: Rare here, everywhere out there
cards.body: The Sun and the other stars are mostly plasma. That makes plasma the most common state of visible matter in the universe: nearly all of it. (That counts ordinary matter, not the mysterious dark matter.) Down here you catch plasma in flashes: lightning, and the glowing curtains of the aurora near the poles. The state you met last is the one the universe uses most.

mascot.line: Solid, liquid, gas: the local specials. Plasma is the house favorite.

cards.headline: One more rung on the energy ladder
cards.body: Remember Level 4: heat makes particles move faster, and melting and boiling are particles breaking free of each other. Plasma is the next rung up. Heat a gas far enough and the breaking goes deeper: electrons break away from their atoms. Solid, liquid, gas, plasma. Each step up is paid for in energy.
cards.callout: Solid → liquid → gas → plasma: more energy at every step

cards.headline: Plasma: sparked
learned: Plasma is a gas of electrically charged particles
Heat or high voltage, like lightning, tears electrons loose

options.label: A gas full of electrically charged particles
A liquid heated to its boiling point
options.rationale: Boiling a liquid makes an ordinary gas.

options.label: A solid that glows in the dark
A gas cooled until it freezes
options.rationale: Plasma needs extra energy, not cooling.

questions.explanation: Plasma forms when electrons are torn from gas atoms, leaving a gas of charged particles.

questions.prompt: Plasma is rare in daily life on Earth, yet it's the most common state of visible matter in the universe. Why?

options.label: Plasma only forms in total darkness
options.rationale: Plasma often glows; darkness isn't needed.

options.label: Earth's gravity crushes plasma into liquid
Only humans can make plasma
options.rationale: Lightning, auroras and stars make it naturally.

options.label: It needs intense heat, and stars supply it

questions.explanation: Tearing electrons loose takes intense heat or voltage. Stars supply that heat, and they hold most of the visible matter there is.

questions.prompt: Level 4 showed heat freeing particles to melt and boil. What does far more heat do to a gas?

options.label: Turns it back into a solid
options.rationale: Adding heat moves matter up the ladder, not down.

options.label: Tears electrons from its atoms, making plasma
Turns it into a liquid
options.rationale: That happens when a gas is cooled.

questions.explanation: Solid, liquid, gas, plasma: each step takes more energy. Enough heat knocks electrons off atoms.
